c.text: This story begins in 1965
Until then, Jupiter, Saturn, Uranus and Neptune, the four giant planets, were a mystery
The problem was distance
Flying straight to Neptune would take about 30 years
No machine, it seemed, could keep working that long
Then Gary Flandro, a young student working at NASA's JPL, worked out the motions of the planets
He saw that between 1976 and 1979, all four planets would line up in a special way
A chance like that comes about once every 175 years
And this line-up had an amazing advantage
When a spacecraft passes a planet, the planet's gravity pulls it and flings it onward
Just as a cricket ball speeds up off a swinging bat
Planet to planet, each time a little more speed
That cut the trip to Neptune from 30 years to just 12
Had they missed it, the next chance would come around 2150

c.text: Until 1979, scientists thought the moons of the giant planets were just cold, dead rock
In March 1979, Voyager 1 reached Jupiter

Her job was to check Voyager's path using the stars
Then she saw a strange cloud at the edge of Io

The first active volcano ever found on any world beyond Earth
Then came Saturn
In 1980, Voyager 1 was sent close to Saturn's moon Titan
Titan has a thick blanket of air, and scientists wanted a close look
But that decision had a price
All the planets circle the Sun on nearly the same flat path, like marbles rolling on a plate
Titan's gravity did what the planets had done before
It bent Voyager 1's path up, out of the plate
Now it could never reach another planet
Voyager 2 made the rest of the journey alone

In that picture, inside a ray of sunlight, is a tiny blue dot
Smaller than a single pixel
That is our Earth
